utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. My laptop is not working, and the same is true for my colleagues, as far as I can see. I think we discussed last Friday there was some need for further communication between the parties. Has this -- has that caused any question to be discussed at this very moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We have not heard from the Defence. And I think there was a deadline of this morning on the communication on the subject of whether the accused would give evidence. But there are also some matters that I seek to raise in private session that I think should take about five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, I think we should turn in to -- perhaps -- I don't know whether the Defence wants to answer to that first question of the Prosecution in open session or would it prefer to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. Thank you. And good day, first of all. But I think it would be better to do that in a hearing which is either a private hearing or a closed hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think private would do for the moment. Mainly, our words not to be heard by the outside world. Could we turn in to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, would you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. DP34. You still can hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. President. I can hear you very clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated. May I remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Pilipovic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. DP34, good day.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We stopped before the weekend with your examination. You were speaking about the fact that at the meeting that you attended in the corps command you said that you would report to your superiors there and analyse the preceding period. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP34, can you tell us whether truce of that had been signed were discussed at those meetings, and can you tell us what you know about truces.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This issue was discussed and they insisted on the fact that such truces should be respected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us as the brigade commander whether in your brigade's zone of responsibility the truce was respected?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you -- did you ever receive reports according to which the truce was violated? Did the enemy side violate a truce or did members of your brigade violate a truce? Did you receive any such reports?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Written reports, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive any reports from your subordinates according to which the enemy side had violated the truce?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in written form; although, they spoke about these minor incidents, so to say. But there weren't any violations of the truce in my zone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "verbal reports," can you be a little more precise and tell us how they reported to you, or rather, what the contents of such verbal reports were when your subordinates reported to you that there were certain skirmishes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me about subordinates?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were regular daily reports if fire was opened, infantry fire, for example, or if a shell fell somewhere, then this was recorded. But when the truces were signed, then during that period there weren't large-scale attacks but there were reports on a daily basis from subordinates, and if fire was opened at a certain part of the line, then this would be reported.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, on the basis of reports according to which fire had been opened, you were able to draw up reports on cease-fire violations.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the basis of such reports provided to you, that is, the information provided to you by your subordinates, did you send any subsequent information to your command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were daily reports to the duty officer of the operations department of the command, and we informed them in detail what had happened the previous day, including any cease-fire violations. They were also reported.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On behalf of the command of your brigade, did you send such reports to the corps command as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have just said, yes, they were sent to the superior command, which was the corps command. Such reports were sent on a daily basis to the duty operations officer. Usually codes would be used and appropriate systems of communication.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at this point the Defence would like to show a document to Mr. DP34.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so. Could the usher assist.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP34, before you have a look at this document, can you please tell us around the 8th of August, 1993 did your brigade form part of the Vogosca Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. DP34, do you recognise the document that has just been put in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a second, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the left corner do we read the words "SRK command"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is the date the 8th of August, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it a regular combat report sent out at 17.00 hours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it sent to the main staff of the Republika Srpska army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please read out item 1.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 1: "The enemy is still not respecting the signed cease-fire."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you confirm for us that the reports on cease-fire violations in your area of responsibility did reach the corps command and that this was written on the basis of reports that had been sent out by specific brigades, that is, from their relevant areas of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that. Specifically, this does not concern my brigade, but it is a regular report, the kind that was usually sent and then forwarded to the main command, to the main staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please slow down, DP34, please, and read item 3 for us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 3: "The situation on the area of responsibility of the corps does not present any significant changes compared to the previous day. The Igman operations and the operations concerning the tactical group of Vogosca are being conducted according to the plan. As far as the area of responsibility of the SRK, flights of NATO aircraft have been sighted."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. DP34. Having read item 3, can you tell us that this would normally also concern the situation as it was in the territory of the area of responsibility of your brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness 34, during the relevant period of time, that is, September 1992 to August 1994, in your brigade's area of responsibility, were there any problems concerning water and power supplies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You said in 1992, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 1992, 1993, up until August 1994.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any problems with water and electricity?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're going far too quick. And I noticed that -- I take it due to the speed, that part of what has been read, I take it, by the witness has not been translated because it reads now that -- and I'm referring to page 16, line 3. It says, "Are being conducted according to the plan," whereas I read in the English translation - and it seems to me that it corresponds with the English language - that mention is made of "the plan Lukavac 93," and where it even says in the English translation but I can't check that, whether it's correct, that the plan Lukavac 93 which is delivered in special report. Is that what it says, Mr. 34?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a second. Item 3. Just a moment. "The situation in the area of responsibility of the corps, no significant changes compared to the previous day. The operations of our units at Igman and TG Vogosca are being conducted according to the Lukavac 93 plan, which is submitted in a special report."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now the interpretation is complete. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just a small remark simply in order to -- no, nothing. Nothing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's a very small remark, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP34, I asked you whether in the area of responsibility of your brigade there were problems concerning water and electricity shortages.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In particular in 1993 there was a long period of time during which -- I think for about seven or eight months that we didn't have any electricity. Electricity lines were improvised at one point in time and the problem was for a certain extent alleviated. The water problem was not that serious because there were sources located in the relevant area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP34, did you personally know what the reasons for power shortages were in your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were shortages on a greater area as well. There was no electricity in the overall area. I guess the power supply lines were cut off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that power supply lines were cut off, do you know how it happened, how it had come about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a unique system of distribution of electric energy, parts of which were towns such as Kakanj, Visegrad, and so on and so forth, and the lines were I guess interrupted, and at one point in time, in particular those around Zvornik, which is not located far from our area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness DP34.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my colleague will take over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your permission, Your Honours. Examined by Mr. Piletta-Zanin:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Witness, good afternoon. I should like to focus on the issue of weapons. Could you tell us if you ever had an opportunity to see for yourself weapons which were not of a fixed nature. And if yes, what -- which weapons they were. I am referring, sir, in particular to the area of Sarajevo which remained under the BH army control.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand your question quite clearly. There were so-called mobile mortars which could be fixed atop of vehicles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as the subject is concerned, can you give us some more information. What types of vehicles in particular were you personally able to observe?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of intelligence information that we disposed of, they were deployed all over the town. They included various types of vehicles, such as a pick-up, a Volkswagen vehicle which was slightly modified but resembled a Golf, for instance; the only difference being a larger trunk. And also 2-tonne trucks, TAM trucks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. For the record, were you speaking about PAM trucks or TAM trucks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: PAM is a completely different thing. It's a -- it's a weapon. TAM is a motor vehicle, 2, 2 and a half tonne motor vehicle, and PAM is an anti-aircraft machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, do you know at which specific locations was it possible for you or your troops to observe these types of vehicles? I'm still referring to the same part of the town.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The area of Betanija, Sip, south of Betanija, actually, and the area of Kosevo, and also the neighbourhood that stretches all the way to Panjina Kula, although we had information to the effect that they were moving around the town, but this was something that we could not specifically observe. We saw mortars all around that area. They would appear very briefly, open fire, and then take shelter behind buildings. Sometimes they wouldn't -- they wouldn't open fire at all but we were able to see them move around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just told us that they would take shelter behind buildings. What type of buildings do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they took various kinds of shelter: Buildings, or hills, or different trees or some other type of shelter, including, of course, houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A moment ago you mentioned Kosevo. Were you referring to the actual hill or something else? I don't know, a particular building that would have been referred to as Kosevo.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The vehicles moved around the streets often, that is, wherever it was possible for them to move, because there were roads in the area, of course, so they would move along the road, the street, or a larger parking lot, wherever it was possible for them to move.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In this area, the area of Kosevo that you've just described, are you aware of the existence of any cemetery? And if yes, which one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said "Kosevo," I was referring to the larger area of Kosevo. There is Kosevo I and Kosevo II. There is a residential area of Kosevo, but that one is also located in the centre. There were cemeteries. There was a cemetery called Kosevo that existed before the war; I think that its name was Kosevo. It existed before the war, but it was no longer active because a new cemetery had been opened in the meantime in the area of Bare.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have just one additional question that I wanted to ask you. And your answer was not recorded in the transcript. I'm interested in the mono-religious or multi-religious character of the cemetery. Were there cemeteries that organised various types of services, various types of religious services that would have been conducted at the same location, at the same cemetery?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several cemeteries in this area, which was relatively small, and several religious communities were buried there. There was a Catholic cemetery, an Orthodox one not far from the centre of the town, then there was this so-called Lav cemetery, which was a Partizan or an atheist cemetery. There was a Muslim cemetery as well. In any case, there were several cemeteries in the same area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should like to focus to the police force now, Witness DP34. What can you tell us about their involvement in fighting? I am speaking of the enemy forces, of course. So in light of your experience, what can you tell us about the engagement of the police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the police is concerned, there were so-called manoeuvre police units before the war which were essentially military in character and were intended to perform tasks which are normally performed by the military. So there were such police units which were normally used together with the military, with the same types of assignments, the same types of tasks. I cannot talk specifically about these tasks because I am not familiar with that, but I know that both police and military units would participate in attacks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Would they wear uniforms? And if yes, what kind and what was the colour of their uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again it all depends on various periods of the war. I am -- it applies to our side as well. They wore blue and camouflage uniforms. There were also standard police uniforms that were worn by the former Yugoslav or BH police before the war, but then after a while probably they obtained some different uniforms, including camouflage uniforms, which I guess were of better quality. But at any rate, there was a difference between police and military uniforms, but the main colour was always blue. As far as our units -- police units are concerned, and their units as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let us now move on to enemy attacks. To the effect that a particular attack is important, can you tell us, did they take place more during the night or during the day or equally? I am, of course, speaking of the enemy forces.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a difference, not only in terms of night and day but also in terms of length of time. They were the fiercest at the beginning of the war and during the night. It is well known that the other side had sabotage and manoeuvre units. I don't think that they were particularly well trained, but they were certainly able to conduct attacks during the night. At the beginning, those attacks took place every day, but later on their intensity decreased. So as far as the period -- the relevant period of time is concerned, I think the attacks had already decreased in their intensity. The fiercest one having been perpetrated at the beginning of the war and during the night, which caused us significant problems. We were even obliged to engage dogs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. You told us that it caused you significant problems. You will tell us what kind of problems, but tell us, please, first of all, as far as these night attacks are concerned, what were the measures that your brigade, your army or your corps, had to take in order to prevent -- of course these attacks or to prevent them in resulting in a victory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we involved everyone, everyone we could get hold of, even young boys, women, and dogs because dogs can sense the approach of troops. It happened mostly during the night, but most of them again were perpetrated right before dawn, at 4 or 5.00 a.m. So of course we didn't want to be surprised. That is, of course, the most efficient defence. If you're able to uncover an approaching attack on time, then that's the most efficient defence that you can have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After this initial phase, once the attack takes place anyway, what were the steps that you were able to take, in particular during the night, in order to fend off the attack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would open barrage fire. Mines were also laid sometimes. We had very efficient explosive devices which were laid in front of the trenches and which could be activated manually with the use of batteries. Hand-held rocket launchers, the so-called tromblons were very efficient, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Speaking of barrage fire and what has been translated to me as "hand-held rocket launchers," as far as the French transcript is concerned, what can you tell us about the use of these means and this type of equipment during the night? Specifically, can you tell something about the use of mortars?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, could you please check whether on line -- page 23, line 14 and following where you say, "What has been translated to me as "hand-held rocket launchers," I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. That's why I mentioned the French transcript. I was listening to the French interpretation, not -- I was not paying attention to the B/C/S words of the witness. I think that the translation was hand-held rocket launcher and not the rifle launcher. But perhaps I can rephrase the question and put it once again in order to avoid confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your permission, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said, "And so on and so forth," Witness DP34, we perhaps had a problem in interpretation. Could you briefly give us a list of weapons other than small arms, such as guns and rifles. What other types of weapons did you have as far as shelling is concerned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me first respond to His Honour the Presiding Judge, because I think that's exactly what I said. I was not referring to mortars. I was referring to rifle launchers, hand-held launchers, which is a standard type of weapon that the former JNA had. It was somewhat dated, but it proved to be very efficient, and it is fired by holding this rifle launcher on the shoulder, and its range is 400 or 500 metres. It is designed to bring about destruction of fortifications and vehicles. But it proved to be excellent in its use against infantry forces, also because it had a major psychological impact. So that was the kind of weapon that I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness DP34. But were there also mortars in your unit? I think you mentioned something to that effect, but I would like to hear it once again clearly, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, although not at the beginning. Depending on the period of time that you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These weapons at the beginning of the war and then later, after September 1992 and the subsequent months, were these particular weapons used and when would they be used during these attacks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In September we did have mortars. We had 60-millimetre, 80-millimetre mortars, and we had one 120-millimetre mortar. But at the beginning we didn't have any ammunition for it, but we did for the other ones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When one uses these weapons, what is the possible margin of error? I'm referring to the mortars. What could you tell us about this, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the margin of error, you are referring to the target?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is always possible. Errors are always possible, depending on how well trained the crew is, and it also depends on how properly the weapon functions. It depends on the quality of the mortar shell and it depends on the weather, on whether it was windy, et cetera, because the shell could be carried to the left or to the right. There are quite a few factors that could cause errors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What could you tell us with regard to the margin of error itself? Not the possibility of errors but the margin of error. I'm asking for a general response.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection. Lack of foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'll rephrase that by asking the witness what he knows about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, as a member of the military, did you know anything about this type of problem that could arise when mortar shells are fired; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know that such errors can occur, but there were no particular problems. For that very reason we didn't use mortars that much because we trusted weapons that could be used for direct fire. They proved to be the most efficient type of weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. With regard to this matter, and in relation to the part of the town that was in front of your units, what can you tell us about targets, in inverted commas, such as mosques or other buildings of a symbolic nature?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are quite a few such buildings in the town of Sarajevo, not only religious buildings but also cultural buildings which UNESCO -- protected by UNESCO, hospitals and so on. They were mostly concentrated in the densely inhabited part of the town in the centre of the town and we didn't open fire on these buildings. It was not necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'll put the question differently, and could you please focus on it. In technical terms, the buildings that you mentioned, the cultural, religious, or symbolic buildings, were any of these buildings or some of them within the range of your weapons? And I'm not saying you fired on these buildings, but were they in range?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, I would now like to go back to certain technical issues which concern mortars. You spoke about barrages of fire. I asked you about the possible margin of error. When you fired barrages, was this from your lines or from the rear of your lines? What was the position from which fire was opened if you were attacked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we were attacked, fire would be opened from the front lines primarily, and then some fire would be opened from behind the lines. Light machine-guns would be used, machine-guns. That would be fire coming from the rear, and it would go over our trenches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, when such fire was opened, was it also possible for errors to be made, technically speaking?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, there was the danger of opening fire on our positions. That was a possibility. Such things happen, and it's dangerous because weapons are used from positions which are just in front of the first lines. That's the danger. But at the first line no errors are possible. That's up to 500 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I'm interested now in General Galic himself. I think that you had the opportunity of meeting him on several occasions in the course of the war. Could you tell us approximately how many times you met him.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't give you a precise number, but I would see him about once or twice a month. But I really don't know the exact number. But to be more precise, that was while I was commander of --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. The approximate figure is quite all right. Thank you. At these meetings that you had with General Galic, you certainly gained the image of -- or the impression of -- a certain impression of your commander. I am interested in this impression, and I would like you to tell us what impression General Galic left on you. Was he of a liberal nature? Was he hard-core, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to apologise. It's not really customary for a subordinate to assess a commander, but we all knew that he was highly educated, that he had finished all schools that could be finished in the former Yugoslavia in the army, and that he performed his duties with competence. I think he was someone who could be characterised as liberal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. With regard to this matter, could you tell us whether you have ever heard a plan of some kind being discussed, the objective of which was to destroy the town or the non-Serb population living in the town.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And I did say "at any possible level" -- "from any level," not just from General Galic, but in your immediate surroundings too. Is this how we are to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, I would like to ask you certain questions about the sites where humanitarian aid was distributed. Do you know anything about the existence of such sites; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the zone in front of me? Yes, we did know that humanitarian aid was being distributed, but we weren't aware of the precise locations, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you on occasion see queues, people waiting for something, I don't know what, perhaps for bread or water, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. That was in the centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you. I would now like you to go back to the number of soldiers in your brigade. Could you remind us of the approximate number and the average, because I assume that this figure changed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the course of the entire war, about 1011 soldiers passed through the brigade, but they were usually between 7 and 8 hundred of them. That would be the highest number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, as someone who was in command -- or for someone in command, given the number of men under your orders, either directly or indirectly, was it possible for them to be entirely familiar with everything that was happening on the lines?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're referring to the commander?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When exercising the post of a commander.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At a given point in time, he can't know everything. Certain information can be found out in the course of the day or the next day, et cetera. But he must have the most important information as far as this is possible, but it's physically impossible for him to have an entire overview of -- a complete overview of the entire line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you develop that a bit, please. Even though this may seem obvious to you, could you expand on that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I am claiming that this is the case. The commander's main task is to command, and this includes receiving reports from subordinate units, his subordinate commanders. It includes receiving reports and orders from his superior command. A commander must take care of and follow the work of all the command organs, and this will have to do with communications, logistics, the medical section. There are many such tasks. And although the line was not very long, the unit whose commander I was did not have a very long line, so it was easier to have an overview of the line, to be familiar with it. But as far as your question as to whether a commander can be totally familiar with the entire situation, my answer is no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Speaking about your line, which was fairly short, can you tell us if you are aware of this how long the front was, which was the responsibility -- the front line which was the responsibility of General Galic. Could you even give us an approximate figure?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how long it was, but we had a look at the map. There was the interior front and there was the external front.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If you don't know, you don't know. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't give you a number in kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, a minute ago you said that it was impossible to know everything. You said this with relation to a certain level. My question is the following: Would this be possible at the level of the command itself? Would it be possible to be familiar with the situation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is my personal opinion that the longer the front line is, the greater the unit is. It's more and more difficult for a commander to be familiar with the situation. He needs more time to gather information in order to be aware of what is happening at the front. He has to receive information from several units, from brigades, from regiments, from independent units. Information has to be obtained from all these formations and this requires time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. At the level of the brigade - and I am speaking in general terms now - Witness, who is in charge of ammunition, and I am referring to all kinds of weapons, and in particular to the weapons that you mentioned, weapons used for shelling in particular?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Logistics, the rear. They have direct contact with the commander, the assistant commander for logistics. So it's the logistics unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you referred to the commander, are you referring to the brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the brigade commander. Or if it concerns other units, the commanders of other units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you yourself have an idea of the amount of ammunition that would be used for certain kind of fire? For example, let's imagine that it was necessary to fire mortars for about five minutes? In such a case, how much ammunition would one use, et cetera, et cetera? Do you have any personal knowledge about this, even if this knowledge is only approximate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't provide you with precise information about that, but this depends on a whole series of circumstances. It depends on the calibre of the weapon. It depends on the capability of the crew, of those charging the mortar, 60-millimetre mortar, because a 60-millimetre mortar can be used for bursts of fire almost. 20-millimetre fire can't be -- can't fire so rapidly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You said a minute ago that you also had machine-guns in your brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would these be what we call heavy machine-guns? For example, that have a calibre of 12.7 millimetres or more?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These were machine-guns that had a calibre up to 12.7 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, this is a purely hypothetical question, but if you had had to use a barrage of fire, to fire a barrage from the weapons that you had from the part of your front line for about 20 minutes in continuity, do you have any idea how much ammunition you would have used in such a case? Have you understood my question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have. This would happen quite often. Attacks would last for even more than 20 minutes. Sometimes the attack would last throughout the day in our direction. You have a combat set then. For example, the infantry would use an entire combat set, 150 bullets, for example. An M-70 automatic rifle would use about that amount of bullets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see or did you have any knowledge of a barrage of fire which was allegedly opened by all the SRK forces on the 24th of December, 1992 and simultaneously against the town; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's the first time I've heard about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If such fire had been opened from your lines, at the level of your brigade, would this have resulted in an imbalance, as far as ammunition is concerned? And yet again, this is a hypothetical question. If you fire -- if there is a barrage of fire opened for 20 minutes in continuity and this fire is directed against Sarajevo, would this have been felt at the level of the ammunition?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, obviously, but I don't know why we would have done such a thing. That would seem that some sort of victory was at stake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, my question is as follows: Did you ever observe in the surroundings on the 24th of December, 1992 any orders for ammunition that would have had to do with the event that I have just described; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't remember anything like that. This question is a bit strange, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, I apologise but I have to ask: Since the 24th is the date of Catholic Christmas, I'm going to ask you the same question for the Orthodox Christmas. What would your reply be?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now the question is clearer to me. As far as holidays are concerned in general --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like you to understand my question, Witness. The 24th is Catholic or even Protestant Christmas. That's the date. Would you give me the same answer if we were talking about Orthodox Christmas?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to answer the question as to holidays. Could you please, where you said "as far as holidays are concerned in general," could you please continue your answer. Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. As far as holidays are concerned, we were warned on several occasions about being in a state of heightened alert from the corps because there were certain indications according to which the enemy side could then take advantage of the festivities, let's call them that, and try and penetrate the line and so on. I remember that. But as far as opening fire is concerned, they opened it a lot more before the war and after the war. But then to a lesser extent, for that very reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But, Witness, you haven't fully understood my question. My question is the same, and this is purely hypothetical: Was there a situation which resembled the one that I have described but not on the Catholic Christmas but on Orthodox Christmas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not -- no such fire. Perhaps there were individual shots -- but no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, I would now like to turn to the other side of the line, the one that you defended. Do you know whether there were any hospitals -- any field hospitals in your territory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our territory, yes. Throughout the war there was the Dr. Ernest Green hospital, it was an active hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Without providing too much information, too many names, et cetera, what can you tell us about what may have happened in relation to this hospital? Were there any problems that arose there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the hospital was run by the Ministry of Health. It was a civilian hospital. But it also treated the entire population, and this included civilians and members of the military.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Was this -- were there any problems with regard to this hospital? Were there any military incidents or something of that nature?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection, relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: May I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the relevance might come from the answer of the witness. So I would first like to ask the witness to tell us whether there were any military incidents or something of that nature in respect of the hospital just mentioned to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was occasionally exposed to mortar fire, but the most significant incident in my opinion was when the doctor was killed -- or rather, the director of that hospital. You told me that I shouldn't mention any names. I know the name, but I don't know whether I should mention his name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mundis, the Chamber might be in a better position now. It's -- the question was about an incident where someone was killed. What would make that less or more relevant than other incidents that have been dealt with in the examination of witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution will withdraw the objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, were there any reasons to target this hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you say "no," how do you explain the fact that shells or other types of ammunition fell on the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection, calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The witness does not know about any targets. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, perhaps the witness should take his headphones off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we'll do it differently. It's quarter to 4.00. We'll discuss the objection upon -- I'll first ask the witness to be escorted out of the courtroom. We'll then hear further about the objection and then -- Yes. The curtains first have to be pulled down, Mr. Usher. If you'll wait for one second. Yes. Would you please follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, do you wish me to -- wish to hear me now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The witness has left the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very briefly. Very briefly. Thank you very much. Our position is as follows: The witness responded to my question that he saw no reason why there should have been shelling, including a military reason as far as the position of the hospital is concerned and so on and so forth. It is possible, and again this is a speculation, that this witness knows if it was a mistake, in terms of targeting, that something else was being targeted, or perhaps that it was a faulty manoeuvre or maybe the witness knows something about this fact. Our position is quite clear, as far as weapons are concerned. It's always possible to make an error, and I think that the Defence has an obligation to demonstrate specifically that such errors could have taken place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand. Well, first of all, targeting errors that are possible, that is similar like whether it's possible that it rains. I think it needs no further explanation. You didn't ask whether he has any knowledge as to where the shells came from, et cetera, which would be a factual approach, but you said, "How can you explain." You didn't even ask the witness whether he could explain but how he would explain. This explanation might be of some relevance if there would be certain specific knowledge. And I take it, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, that if you put these kind of questions to a witness that you might have discussed this prior to his testimony. So then you could ask him about whether he knew who exactly would have fired that shot. Or if you keep it to facts, then we stay out of the domain of speculation and certainly Mr. Mundis would have no reason to object to your question. So if you would like to explore this matter, I think there would be no objection against that. But then please start with the facts and then finally we'll find out whether the witness has an explanation and what his explanation will be.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll break until twenty minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we resume the examination of the witness, there are a few issues. The first one is a very practical one. The Chamber is made aware of the fact that we could sit tomorrow in the morning instead of the afternoon. The Chamber would not oppose to that, and it's generally felt that sitting in the morning is more attractive than sitting in the afternoon. But I would like first to hear from the parties whether there would be any objection against sitting in the morning rather than in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No objection from the Prosecution, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The general is nodding no, so I took that that you have no objections other. So then we'll sit tomorrow morning. There has been another request to sit on Friday in the afternoon. And apart from other problems, would that find objections as far as the parties are concerned? That would be we change from the afternoon to the morning and now the Chamber was requested to change again from the morning to the afternoon. And there are other problems as well. But I'd just like to know how the parties would respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, could the Prosecution reserve getting back to you on that until after the next break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try to check, Mr. President. It has to do with my trip back. If you are talking about Friday, I don't know the time of my flight. I understand that it costs a lot if we change the schedule, if I change the reservation. So with that proviso --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- might be opposed by the parties, and I had in mind that you might have to travel over the weekend, so -- and there are other reasons why this request might fail to work out well. But I just wanted to know from the parties. Then as far as two other issues are concerned: Whatever instructions the Chamber has given to the parties on informing the Prosecution and the Chamber on the appearance of witnesses, as long as such instructions have not been withdrawn, they stand. That means that whatever the Chamber has instructed the parties to do, irrespective of what the Chamber could still expect, that as long as they have not been withdrawn, we continue as -- as we have decided. Then finally, the translation of annexes. On the 26th of November, Ms. Pilipovic, you have clearly indicated that you would solve the problem of the translation of the annexes. If my learned colleague insists on having certain texts and articles translated into one of the official languages of the Tribunal, I can solve this problem too. My colleague and I will sit down and we'll solve this problem. That's what the Chamber expects the parties to do. That means the Defence to assist in solving the problem and to sit together perhaps and find out what will be the priorities. Those are our decisions. Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, in light of the first decision with respect to timetable and scheduling of witnesses, the Prosecution would respectfully request from the Chamber additional guidance to the Defence with respect to the issue of whether the accused will be testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could the Defence indicate when it intends to give this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we will meet, first of all, with General Galic. And once we have had an opportunity of calmly discussing the situation, in light of the overall information that we have, I think that we will be able to provide you with the response either tomorrow or the day after tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, if this information would be available by next Wednesday, would that cause insurmountable problems?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: By Wednesday meaning of this week or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of this week, yes. We're talking about tomorrow or the day after tomorrow, so that's Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That's -- that's certainly acceptable, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then -- yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. President, Ms. Pilipovic is reminding me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We earlier discussed a matter in private session. Is there any specific need to have everything redacted? I see, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you are nodding no. The nodding of Ms. Pilipovic is not quite clear. We didn't go into any content of it. Yes. Okay. Then we'll leave it as it is. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Ms. Pilipovic is reminding me that the deadline is seven days, that the Defence is under the obligation to inform whether this testimony will take place or not within seven days. So why should it not be in the case of this witness? Because that is the normal procedure in case of other witnesses. So we would like to stick to this if this is possible. If the witness expresses his willingness to testify, then you will be notified of his decision within seven days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This system is a different one. I think that as latest seven days prior to the testimony of the witness the summary should be made available. I think that the system is that witnesses are on the list. You have put a witness on the list and you reserve the right. You said you were not sure. We accepted that at that time. Usually if someone is to be added to the list, permission has to be asked. And I would say that we should -- that the Prosecution should have sufficient time for cross-examination. That's not an easy task to prepare, I would say. We -- I asked last week when you would provide this information. You said by today. And for reasons you have explained, you said you would not do so today. Then we asked the Defence when they would provide this information, and the answer was by tomorrow or the day after tomorrow. That is a fair way of dealing with it. So there is no general rule that you give notice seven days in advance on whether a witness will appear or not. Then is the Defence ready to continue the examination of the witness? Could the usher be assisted in pulling down the curtains by Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 17880 to 17889. whatever forces that are available in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In application of what you said, Witness, do you know perhaps not who exactly but which side it was that shelled the hospital that we mentioned before the break?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The opposing side. They shelled the hospital on the 27th of July, 1993, sometime around noon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, to the extent that -- well, according to your testimony, there were no military targets in or around the hospital, could you explain to us why according to your knowledge this shelling took place.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not in the position to know that. It is true that the hospital is located relatively close to the front lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean by "relatively close"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say that it was located relatively close to that area, I mean that it was possible to target the hospital with infantry weapons, such as semi-automatic rifles. It was -- light machine-guns.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far approximately was this hospital located from the front-line trenches, approximately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1.000 metres approximately. That would have been the closest distance, as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, apart from what you just said, that the hospital was relatively close to the trenches, to the front lines, are there any other reasons why it should have become a target, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mundis -- Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you answer my question, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can answer your question. Do you mean in the vicinity of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from the distance problem, that is, the fact that the hospital was located relatively close to the front line, were there any other reasons why this hospital should have become a target, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. I understand -- I understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One moment, please. Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The question was asked and answered. I refer to page 42, line 15, the first sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague is quite right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us move on to another subject. With respect to a document which I would like to show to you in a moment -- but let me start with the question. Can you tell us precisely what documents, what documentation could have been found at the brigade, the documents in connection with humanitarian law, that is, in connection with the Geneva Conventions in particular?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From our superior command, we received on several occasions orders regarding the respect of the Geneva Conventions, which were then transmitted to subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you perhaps be more precise and give us a few more details regarding the issue. What type of instructions are we talking about here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received written instructions printed on an A4 paper, which we then copied and then transmitted to subordinate units. There were cases when these instructions were posted on the entrances to the trenches. One of the commanding officers was surprised to see one such document posted on the entrance to a trench, alongside other documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us focus on this document specifically. You said that they were usually printed on an A4 piece of paper. What exactly was it? Was it just a resume, a summary of the document, or the entire document? What exactly was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It consisted of two -- the document consisted of two pages with specific provisions of the Geneva Conventions, including the treatment of civilians, the prohibition of the use of weapons against civilians, the treatment of the wounded, the treatment of the prisoners of war, the prohibition of targeting -- on targeting civilian objects, cultural monuments, and so on and so forth. I don't know -- I don't remember all of the items by heart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. How often did you yourself see such documents being posted in the combat area, in particular in the trenches? How often did you personally see such instructions being displayed in this manner?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally escorted the commanding officer of the Vogosca Tactical Group, and I once saw that in the Klomolj trenches. The commander commended this use, and then others also followed suit. But I remember this specific example as having taken place in the area of Klomolj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned a commanding officer, a commander. Was it an officer who was attached to the corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was quite precise. I said commander of the Vogosca operative group who was visiting the lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the assistance of the usher, I would now like to show you a document, the number of which is 1453, and this will probably be our last line of questions. Naturally, with your permission, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, the first question: Do you recognise this type of document and do you recognise the signature it bears?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this type of document is familiar to me. And there are two signatures here, and I can recognise them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise both signatures? Do you recognise both signatures?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I think both signatures are authentic. This one up here is the general's, and the one under "certified," says "Colonel."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, could you concentrate on item 1. And I am interested in the second paragraph in particular. I don't think it will be necessary to look at the first paragraph, but if you wait for just a minute, I will confer with my colleague. No. We can take the time to do this, so I would appreciate it if you could read the first two paragraphs under item 1.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 1: "Prepare the most persistent and decisive defence on reached lines and by the manoeuvre of forces find appropriate grouping of forces in select directions, improve operative positions of the corps. Cut off the communications of Ustasha forces between Treskavica and Bjelasnica. Unblock the Sarajevo-Trnovo-Dobro Polje road, and the Sarajevo-Srednje-Olovo road, Pazaric-Igman. With liberation and reaching the important parts of the town -- I think it says "reaching" -- structures within its vicinity (Mojmilo, Stupska Petlja) and settlements (Kotorac, Hrasnica, Butmir, Sokolovic Kolonija)."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the second paragraph too, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Stop the weekend war and habits in that sense. Furthermore, defeat the Ustasha's forces in that region of Gorazde, Foca, Visegrad, and make parts for actions --"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. It was just the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A minute ago -- and you can find this in the first line of the first paragraph -- you spoke about the organisation of defence. Can you tell us exactly and in greater detail what this order -- what these instructions mean.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in concrete terms, it's an order to units. A specific task is assigned. Here it says "decisive defence." And then further on it says "the manoeuvre of forces --"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll interrupt you. What does "decisive defence" mean, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Decisive defence" -- in our brigade, I and the commander who came later, our main task was to mount a decisive defence because of the character of the unit, the fact that there weren't many men. So it excludes offensive action of any kind. All it has to do with is the defence of the lines that are established.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, as a member of the military, and given experience that you have had, what is this idea of decisive defence opposed to? What is the opposite of a decisive defence, if you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would be a frontal attack, an attack. That would be the opposite of a decisive defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I would now like to examine the second paragraph, which mentions the weekend war. Those are the terms used in the document. First of all, if this is the case, can you confirm that such orders were issued to you by the command in order to suppress this problem? And if this was the case, how frequently were such orders issued?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, quite frequently -- I'll read it out. "Stop the weekend war and habits in that sense." That means that there were members of the unit who would go away on leave and then they would stay on leave. They would take leave of their own accord. So they used the term "weekend war." For example, you would get two days of leave, but then he would take five days. He would even go to Belgrade and then return. And then he was called a "weekend warrior." That's a term that existed, that was in use. It's something that was condemned or, rather, they insisted on terminating such activities, but such activities were never fully eradicated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Does that mean that an attempt was made in your corps and in particular in your brigade to introduce the most organised possible form of discipline?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the brigade which was under my command is concerned, this was not something that was very widespread. Weekend war was not an issue that was very present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Mr. Mundis, is the Prosecution ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. DP34, you'll now be examined by counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Actually, Mr. Usher, if that document could please remain with the witness for one moment. Cross-examined by Mr. Mundis:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you please turn to the second page of that document and read paragraph numbered 19.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute. Item 19: "Stop robbery, profiteering and other vices that besmirch the reputation of the army and people and cause huge damages."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, Witness, was robbery and profiteering a problem during the time that you were a brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please read paragraph number 20.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Remove persons and those who do not accept an invitation -- runaway persons and those who do not accept the invitation are considered as the most dangerous traitor of his own people and start the procedure of confiscation of his property."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, with respect to the word "invitation" that appears in that paragraph, do you know what that reference is about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a call-up. It has to do with not responding to a call-up to engage in the military. That's what it means. Just a minute. Just a minute. In this specific case -- in this case, within this context, when it says "who do not accept an invitation," it means those who left and who are then asked to return again. So it means those who left and were then asked to return again. Such people are to be considered as traitors. I think that in this context, this reply would be more precise. I think it means those who were in the unit who left were then called to return and didn't return.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the sake of clarity in the transcript, I think it's clear to everyone but nevertheless page 49, line 10 I don't think the witness said "we move," as it says in the transcript. I think it would sooner be the past participle, so that things are clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the interpreters then re-took the translations at persons. Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd ask that we go into private session for a few questions, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll turn in to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in open session again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you told us today that you saw the accused General Galic approximately one or two times per month. I assume that that was in your capacity as a brigade commander; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that throughout the period of the time that you were a brigade commander, that is, during the entire length of your tenure as a brigade commander you saw General Galic once or twice a month?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. Yes. I went to regular meetings at which commanders were present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these meetings held at the corps headquarters at Lukavica barracks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not all of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where else do you recall these meetings taking place, other than Lukavica barracks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they also took place in the western part of Sarajevo, in Butile, I think, there was a barracks in Butile. That's where they were held. There was a ring road. Sometimes it was difficult to get from one part to the other, so the commander would go to the western part. And on Jahorina there were meetings in a hotel there too. That's -- those are the locations I can remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the positions of other individuals who attended these meetings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean all those who attended them?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, those people who attended them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corps command, members of the corps command, the brigade commanders, the commanders of independent regiments and battalions who were part of the corps, so directly subordinated to the corps. There were others too, but as far as the military structure is concerned, that's what was most frequently the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Galic was in effect the chair of these meetings; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any of these meetings, either at Lukavica barracks or any of the other locations that you mentioned, did you ever hear anyone mentioning the topic of protests concerning shelling?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was mentioned. It was said that UNPROFOR had made such suggestions, that UNPROFOR had suggested that there shouldn't be any shelling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these protests that you've just mentioned concerning the shelling of civilians and civilian objects such as apartment blocks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that question precisely. I don't know about that. But the subject was discussed, in any event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear anyone at any of these meetings discuss the topics of protests concerning the sniping of civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard them talking about snipers. I heard that they said that they fired at our side, but this wasn't discussed very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall hearing General Galic complain at these meetings about protests that he received concerning the unlawful sniping of Bosnian Muslim civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear General Galic complain about any protests that he received concerning unlawful shelling of Bosnian Muslim civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did General Galic during the time that you were a brigade commander ever visit the area of responsibility that your brigade covered?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was commander, General Galic came to the zone of responsibility on two occasions, but he passed through the zone of responsibility on several occasions. But he came on two occasions when I was commander, and he would pass through towards the western part of the battlefield, towards Vogosca on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the two occasions that General Galic came to your brigade's zone of responsibility, what was the purpose of those visits?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he found out about the situation on the ground. He became familiar with the situation on the ground and with the problems. From the positions, he observed the lines. He issued instructions, orders. As I said, he didn't have any problems with us; he never did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the contents of the instructions or orders that you received from General Galic during the times that he was in your brigade's zone of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He mainly insisted on a decisive defence, and he said that we should at no -- by no means allow the line to be penetrated because in such a case, the enemy forces would advance 10 kilometres or even more. That was his opinion. They would take certain important positions in a northern part of the battlefield. And again, we complained that we didn't have enough men and we said that we needed more men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall on these two occasions that the accused visited your zone of responsibility how long he remained there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to be exact, on the first occasion - that was at the beginning when he came - he spoke very briefly, and it was more a sake of protocol, a matter of introducing himself. And the second time was in 1993, I think -- 1993 or the beginning of 1994. I know it was winter. I can't remember the exact time. But the first time was just when he assumed the post of commander, and he was there for a very brief period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By "brief" do you mean more than or less than one hour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, something like that. About an hour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long was the accused General Galic present on the second occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the second occasion, he spent more time there. As I said, he went to the positions. He came to the forward command post. I forgot to mention that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was the forward command post located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Pretrzanj area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that where your brigade's artillery positions were located as you've described on Friday?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's in the vicinity, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As part of this visit to the command's forward command post, did General Galic visit those artillery positions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was with the officers, and he was only with the officers. He passed by our position. He spoke to the soldiers. But he didn't visit all the positions. UNPROFOR was positioned there too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say "he didn't visit all the positions." Did he visit some of the artillery positions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, on the way he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
