utterances.text: You also told us that he passed through your brigade's zone of responsibility on his way to Vogosca on a few occasions. Did he make any stops in your zone of responsibility during any of those times that he was transiting your brigade's area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that I don't know how many times he transited the area because he would also escort UNPROFOR through the town. But he didn't get in touch with me on those occasions, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based on the meetings that you attended at Lukavica barracks and other places where General Galic presided and the times he visited your command, were you able to make an assessment as to whether or not General Galic had a good grasp of events occurring within the corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the corps. But as far as my brigade is concerned, I think he had a full grasp of the situation because his subordinate officers, that is, assistant commanders of the corps, often came to the area. Members of his staff, they frequently visited the area, and it is my assumption that they would convey to him what the situation was, in addition to the regular reports that we sent out. I don't know about other brigades.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based on the meetings that you attended where information was passed up and down the chain of command, was General Galic receiving sufficient information to keep himself informed about events that were occurring in the corps's area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The expression "about events" is not precise enough. It's much too wide for the witness to answer the question, and I think the questions should be limited to the subject discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'll rephrase the question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, what type of information was relayed from the brigade commanders or other senior subordinate officers to General Galic during the meetings that you attended at Lukavica or other locations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only answer so far as my brigade is concerned, if we're talking about all reports. Are you referring only to what was specifically discussed at the meetings or generally speaking? Are you including in this the written reports that were relayed, that we sent out to the corps? That's what I'm not clear about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me attempt to explain. You attended meetings once or twice a month for a period of more than one year, and during these meetings the brigade commanders, members of the corps staff were in attendance. What matters -- what issues do you recall being discussed at these meetings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I fully understand what you mean. First of all, the brigade commanders would submit a written report, a kind of briefing, either oral or on paper, but they would usually read out their reports on what the situation was in the territory of their units, including the situation as it was at the front line, the problems with which the unit was faced, including logistics, lack of ammunition, problems with communication equipment, the quartermaster issues, and other similar problems that would arise within a unit. They would also submit their proposals as to how a situation should be resolved. They made such proposals to the commanders, and then members of the corps command, depending on their relevant department, would also submit their reports. For example, the assistant commander for logistics or the assistant commander for intelligence, they would make their appropriate reports, and then the corps commander would make a summary thereof, give his opinion, and issue guidelines or orders as to what should be done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall at any of these meetings if General Galic ever asked questions or engaged any of the briefers on issues that they discussed at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Speaking of myself, for example, to be as specific as possible, I always insisted on the problem of shortage of manpower. And the response I would usually get was that there were no -- enough people and that I should make the best possible use of what I had. Others had other types of problems. The corps commander would sometimes describe how our unit was doing, how we were able to manage as best as we could with the little troops that we had, so he would give us as an example. So those were the kinds of things that he discussed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, Witness, if the corps had liaison officers whose job it was or whose area of responsibility was dealing with UNPROFOR and other UN personnel in the theatre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the area of the corps, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall if the liaison officer or officers attended the meetings that you attended once or twice a month with the corps commander and others?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did attend such meetings, but I don't know whether it was at all such meetings. I don't know whether they always attended. I guess it was whenever it was necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the liaison officer or officers raising issues concerning protests or complaints at the meetings that you attended in which General Galic was presiding?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would inform him on the problems that they were faced with. There were lots of such meetings, the meetings between UNPROFOR and the belligerent parties. There were many such contacts, and they were in charge of that, so that was the only topic that they discussed, nothing else. That is, what had been agreed at a particular meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based on the subjects that were discussed at these meetings, did it appear to you that the corps commander, General Galic, had a good grasp with respect to these issues that we've been discussing, everything from logistics, personnel issues, complaints received by the UN, et cetera? Based on your attendance at the meetings, did it seem to you that he had a good grasp of these issues?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had that feeling. Sometimes the situation would be explained by the relevant officer, the officer in charge of a specific department. If, for example, the problem discussed was a logistics problem, then the assistant commander for logistics would address it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, based on your attendance at these meetings, do you ever recall an instance at any of these meetings where the subject of non-compliance with the corps commander's orders was raised?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Non-compliance with the orders coming from the corps command? Is that what you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in that form. There were, if I may explain, as far as I remember, discussions as to whether a particular commander had fully complied with an order, had fully acted pursuant to an order, but not as to whether he had complied with the order at all. At least, not to my recollection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you ever recall at any of these meetings the corps commander, General Galic, getting upset or angry because any of his orders were not carried out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think he was always very calm. No. No, not that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear about any instance in which General Galic became angry or upset because his orders weren't being carried out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not with respect to non-compliance with the orders. Not with respect to that, at least.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, how did your brigade typically receive its orders from the corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The orders were usually in written form, that is, a written order issued by the corps commander to defend. So that was the standing order from the very beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you say "the orders were usually in written form." That implies that there were also periodic oral orders. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said a moment ago, during the meetings and the regular briefings, oral tasks were sometimes given. But in principle, they were in writing. That is, as I said, the standing order was to defend, and then we had orders concerning the external line of defence and similar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall ever receiving any kind of standing order regarding sniping of civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I have to say we did not have sniper rifles. We had no need for such weapons. As far as our lines are concerned, everything could be achieved with normal weapons, as far as all sides are concerned. Later on we used automatic weapons for fighting. So the sniping, as it is usually referred to and as it is often used in war, as far as our brigade line is concerned, there were no such cases on either side. Although, we had more than ten casualties on our side, and the explanations sometimes were sniping. But in most of the cases these casualties were the result of normal fire, fire from normal, ordinary weapons. But every time when there was no real fighting, no real conflict, the term that was used would be "sniping." But that was really not the case. As far as our side is concerned, it was, practically speaking, impossible to use them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, a few moments ago you said "the standing order was to defend, and then we had orders concerning the external line of defence and similar." Do you recall any other standing orders issued by the corps that would apply to all the subordinate units of the corps, any other standing orders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, a standing order was decisive defence. Whether other brigades had the same order, I don't know, but in case of my brigade that was the basic order to be followed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't recall any other standing orders issued by the corps that applied to all the subordinate units of the corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me a moment ago about snipers, if that's what you have in mind. Our unit didn't have any such weapons, and I think that the same is implied with respect of other units. The Geneva Conventions provide for prohibition on targeting civilian persons. As to whether there was a specific standing order to that effect, I don't know. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, your brigade made daily reports -- daily written reports to the corps headquarters; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our brigade made daily reports to the duty operations officer. We also submitted brief oral reports and also written reports that were submitted through the Vogosca Brigade, because we didn't have the code. We did not have daily written reports, but we did have reports made on a daily basis in one way or another. It was customary for the brigade duty operations officer to report daily to the corps duty operations officer and to inform him briefly on the situation or on what had happened the previous day. If there was anything important to be conveyed to the corps, then such reports were made in writing by using the coded language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: One more question, Mr. President, then a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, these -- you said "customary for the brigade duty operations officer to report daily to the corps duty operations officer." Was this reporting done at a certain time every day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that it was customary. It was an obligation for the duty officer of the brigade to inform regularly the duty officer of the corps. It was always done as a specific time of the day; for instance, between 8.00 and 9.00 in the evening. Actually, I don't think that the time was always the same during the war, but they knew when to expect a report. Also, one hour prior to that time, the subordinate units would report to the brigade command so that the brigade command could collate the information and then transmit it to the corps. That was the procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll adjourn until five minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While waiting until the witness will be brought in, document 1453, we -- it's a relatively short document of which we only received the first and the third page. Could the second page be provided as well so that we can relate the first page with the third page with the -- yes. Mr. Mundis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I believe you told us on Friday that the Vogosca Operational Group subsequently became the Vogosca Tactical Group. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you receive translation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you know why the Vogosca Operational Group was first formed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Vogosca Operational Group was formed at the very beginning. As far as I can recall, it was sometime in early May. I don't know the exact date. I don't know who issued the order as to its establishment, but the reason why it was formed was, I think, because it was assessed that it would be easier to mount a defence in this manner. But it is possible that there were other reasons as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Vogosca Operational Group was commanded by Vukota Vukovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I actually have a question for you, Your Honours. May I? May I ask a question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said on Friday that when names need to be mentioned that I can request a private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you rather respond to this question in private session as far as -- if I understand you well? Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I mean, I think you said it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would like to ask for one now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would be hesitant to mention a name, you could ask for private session. That's what I told you. Here, of course, the name already is mentioned. But nevertheless, if even for confirming or denying that he was, you would prefer to go into private session -- looking at the parties, there seems to be no major objection --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll turn in to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in open session again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, how frequently did you have dealings with Lieutenant Colonel Jusipovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean while the tactical group was still in existence?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: During that period? Quite frequently. Quite frequently. Because there were meetings which were held quite often.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have daily contact with him during this period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not daily meetings, but this took place very frequently, far more frequently than with the corps command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your brigade receive targeting orders from Lieutenant Colonel Jusipovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please be more specific. Which targets are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your unit receive orders from that individual to engage enemy forces or positions held by the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And this is something I have already said. Our task was never to carry out an attack. We never received such orders. We only put aside part of our forces for the outer ring, part of the forces which at the Nisici plateau. But we didn't carry out an attack against the Federation army in the course of the war. The brigade never carried out an attack, neither on its own or in cooperation with someone else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your brigade --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would just like to intervene because part of the witness's response was not translated to -- it doesn't appear in the French translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please check with the English translation whether that's complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The English translation is complete inasmuch as it refers to what happened in the case of the external ring, and this does not appear in the French translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your observation as such will cause those who are working on the transcript to be very alert. Please proceed, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you told us that your brigade did not carry out any attack against the Federation army during the war. Did your brigade in any way engage the Federation army during the course of the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. How else would there have been so many wounded and dead in the brigade? I said that last time, and I've said it today too. There was a period during which attacks were carried out on a daily basis. Most of them took place at night. Gradually the number of attacks diminished, yes. There was fierce fighting. For example, if several men died on our side and we didn't have any information about how many died on their side and if there were tens of wounded, then that's a conflict. That's engagement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to these engagements, did your unit receive any orders -- specific orders regarding targeting from Lieutenant Colonel Jusipovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the tactical group was established and while it existed, I don't know how many months it was in existence exactly, but during that period there weren't very many frontal attacks in our direction. It was one of the calmer axes on the Sarajevo battlefield.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you ever receive any orders from Lieutenant Colonel Jusipovic that troubled you with respect to their legitimacy or lawfulness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in the sense that civilians were targeted? Are you referring to civilian features and features that according to the Geneva Conventions must not be targeted?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's start with that category. Did you ever receive any orders from Lieutenant Colonel Jusipovic concerning targeting of civilians that caused you concern?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I never received such an order from anyone, and I never issued such an order, nor would I ever do such a thing. I'm referring to indiscriminately targeting civilian features. That would be totally senseless.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I put to you that Lieutenant Colonel Jusipovic condoned the targeting of unlawful targets and specifically civilians. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I can tell you that while Lieutenant Colonel Jusipovic was the commander of the tactical group, that was a unit that covered almost the entire northern -- north-western battlefield and the western battlefield. If you have any such information, I can't comment on it. There were a number of firing positions, a number of units which were part of the tactical group. It was larger than the operative group, although one might have the other impression given the names. But it had more men and more equipment. So this is not something I could either confirm or deny.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to any other orders, that is, any order whatsoever from Lieutenant Colonel Jusipovic, did any order that you received from him cause you concern with respect to its legitimacy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Mr. President. Objection, given that it appears that the witness has already answered this question, page 70, line 16. He said he had never received such orders and as a result it's obvious that he could not contest the legitimacy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... whether specific orders were asked for. And then Mr. Mundis said, "Okay. Let's start with the order you indicate." And now he's asking about other orders. The question is whether apart from what you've told us about whether you ever received any orders or whether ever any orders were given by Colonel Jusipovic to target civilians, whether there were ever any other orders -- that means orders not specifically dealing with targeting civilians -- that caused you to think about whether these orders were legitimate or not. So we're not talking now about orders in respect of targeting civilians but any other order, whatever the order might have been about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall receiving any orders from anyone in the Sarajevo Romanija Corps that gave you concern or caused you concern with respect to the legitimacy of that order?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about anything so drastic. There were certain events which appeared on television -- for example, Markale and other similar incidents in which civilians had died. But that has nothing to do with our unit. Whether it has something to do with some unit from the Vogosca Tactical Group, that's something I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us, Witness, on Friday that at one point you were no longer the commander of a brigade but, rather, became the commander of a battalion. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. To be precise, once the operative group -- you mean after the operative group had been disbanded? Is that what you are thinking of?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I said - I was very precise, I think - I said I was the commander of the brigade while it existed. But after that I wasn't in the Kosevo Brigade at all. I assumed another post. I said it didn't even exist. I wasn't in that unit at all. It was part of that brigade. I now remember what you are asking me about. I remember it quite clearly now. When that unit was disbanded as a brigade, it was transformed. Most of it remained as a battalion. I wasn't the commander of that battalion. I think I have understood you now. I think I have been clear. Sir, I never had that position. I assumed a totally different post.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this new post, what were your primary responsibilities or duties?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I'd like to say I went to the 3rd Sarajevo, when it was formed, from the beginning of February. And I was assistant for morale and for information and for legal affairs. That's what it was called. And my responsibility was also to liaise with UNPROFOR. I was the person who would most frequently contact UNPROFOR at the level of the brigade. And I remained at that post until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, at any time when you were a member of the -- of any unit of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps between September 1992 and August 1994, were you ever directed or ordered to conduct any type of investigation concerning unlawful targeting of Bosnian Muslim civilians by any member of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we please stop for one second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm just interested in the question being put in precise terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting. Please proceed. Can we please -- the last question, Mr. Mundis, was whether the witness could clarify. Perhaps you'll resume in such a way that we don't lose anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, during the period from September 1992 through August 1994, while you were the member of subordinate units of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, were you ever directed or ordered to conduct any type of investigation concerning the unlawful targeting of Bosnian Muslim civilians by any member of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question is quite clear to me now. No, I never did receive such orders. But during that period, I think representatives from the main staff even came once or twice, and UNPROFOR representatives, as well as members of the corps, and they checked certain things in our units and in other units. But no complaint was ever made to us as a side that had violated a truce or done something like that, and I think that took place on two occasions. That was with UNPROFOR. But it wasn't an order. All we had -- all we received was an order according to which a certain team would be arriving and that we should allow them to work without hindrance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear at any time between September 1992 and August 1994 that any investigations were carried out within the Sarajevo Romanija Corps concerning unlawful targeting of Bosnian Muslim civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that some kind of action was taken to that effect but I don't know anything more specific about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall any discussions at any of the meetings that you attended where the corps commander was present where the subject of such investigations was discussed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not in detail. And this is something I said just before the break. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall any discussions at any of the meetings that you attended where the corps commander was present where the subject of military prosecutions for the unlawful targeting of Bosnian Muslim civilians was discussed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do I remember whether this was discussed? I remember that they discussed that opening such fire would result in criminal prosecution and other penalties. In particular, attention was drawn to the fact that a lot of damage was being done to our image in the eyes of the International Community. Yes, something to that effect. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall any specific discussions about whether any such prosecutions were undertaken during the time period September 1992 through August 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I know of. At least, not in my brigade. And I'm not aware of the situation in other brigades.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I take it from the fact that you weren't aware of the situation in other brigades that you do not recall ever hearing the issue of prosecutions for these offences being discussed at meetings that you attended in which the corps commander was also present during this period.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said, and I repeat, mention was made at such meetings that in cases of opening non-selective fire on civilian targets such action is very damaging and that the perpetrators could be sanctioned. But that the commander should have -- would have mentioned any names, names of specific commanders? No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me be absolutely clear, Witness. My question is not in general terms that such unlawful targeting damaged the reputations or that it could result in prosecutions. My question is: Do you recall any discussions in which actual Prosecution of individuals for these violations was discussed?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object because quite specifically the question implies something that has not been the testimony of this witness, that is, that such orders were allegedly given and obeyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was whether you have any recollection in which it was discussed to investigate or to prosecute any individual for violation of the prohibition of opening non-selective fire on civilian targets or whatever other violation of the rules. So was there ever any discussion on -- we have to investigate or we should prosecute Mr. X, Y, or Z for what he has done in violation of the rules? Yes, could you please answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question is quite clear. But I never attended such meetings. I mean, it was not discussed when I attended these meetings. It is possible that it happened, but I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, on Friday you told us that you were aware that two murders had occurred and that the individuals responsible were prosecuted; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the facts underlying the prosecution of these individuals?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We didn't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your answer because the interpreters couldn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the crime of murder.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know with respect to either of these individuals charged who the victim was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both perpetrators and victims were soldiers of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the perpetrators prosecuted in civilian courts or in some type of courts martial?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The arrest was carried out by the military police, but the case was then taken to the civilian court, to the civilian jurisdiction at the Kula headquarters where the civilian police was located, and they received several years in prison. I don't know exactly how it ended, but I know that they were tried and convicted in a civilian court and that they were imprisoned in a civilian prison which still exists today and was a civilian prison even before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, Witness, why they were prosecuted in civilian court rather than in a military court or before a court-martial?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that they served their sentences at the civilian court, but I don't know what the outcome of the proceedings was. If that was the case, I think it was because there were no military courts or court-martial in that area, because the state of war had not been declared and courts martial were not established at the level of the unit, at the level of the corps. So what happened later, I don't know. I don't know only that proceedings indeed took place and that they served their sentence at the Lukavica prison, which is under the jurisdiction of the civilian police. This civilian prison had existed prior to the war and it still exists.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any time during September 1992 through August 1994, are you aware of any military courts being set up or anyone being prosecuted by a military prosecutor during that time period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the brigade, that is, in my unit, no. In the Kosevo Brigade and in the 3rd Sarajevo Brigade, no. It was established in 1995 at one point in time, this military court; however, it never reached any judgment and it lasted only a brief period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know when these two individuals were arrested on murder charges?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: One individual at the beginning of the war, either in May or in June - I don't know the exact date - but fairly early in the war. And the second one, in 1994, when I was already a member of the 3rd Sarajevo Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the ranks of the perpetrators and/or the ranks of the victims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were soldiers, both of them, privates, had no rank, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, on Friday you told us that UNPROFOR had their own maps. Did you ever see these maps, these UNPROFOR maps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, several times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall if these UNPROFOR maps included the positions of the parties' forces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, I didn't have full insight in such maps, but occasionally when a member of UNPROFOR would unfold a map and ask us about our combat positions, I was able to see what the situation on the opposing side was, but it was never officially presented to us nor were we ever able to see it in detail. In most of the cases they would show us the situation on our side. But of course from time to time you could glance at the other side as well, when the map was fully unrolled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall if these maps indicated positions before and after the heavy weapons agreement came into force? Were those positions marked on the map or maps that you saw?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They changed, both before and after. My recollection is not very precise. I can only tell you that I am sure that I saw such maps. As for the details, I'm afraid I cannot tell you about the details. After all, it was ten years ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it your understanding that UNPROFOR's role during the heavy weapons agreement was to ensure that the monitored weapons were not used?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And not only the heavy weapons but the overall compliance with the cease-fire agreement, that the area of responsibility should be monitored in order to see if there were any violations, any cases of opening of fire, and similar. And this was relatively easy to control in my area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the fact that the UN as monitors of the heavy weapons agreement was there to ensure that those heavy weapons weren't being used by the parties, did that have any influence or impact upon targeting decisions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I mean, UNPROFOR was present in the immediate vicinity of the weapons for a period of time, and then they also toured the area. They visited the relevant positions. We had received instructions as to our obligation to enable this to UNPROFOR. I don't know if there are any cases of -- if there were any cases of complaints by UNPROFOR as to our possible failure to comply. Such protests never reached me, in any case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, on Friday you mentioned that the Federation army had 81-millimetre and 82-millimetre mortars. Are these different types of mortars?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, I said either 81- or 82-millimetre mortars, and I said that because practically these are two same types of weapon. You can only identify which weapon had fired if you have an unexploded shell. In other cases, you can identify the firing weapon on the basis of shrapnel or fragments, but not in the case of these two weapons. They have equal capabilities, the same performance. The only difference is the radius of the shell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you know if the Federation army had both 81- and 82-millimetre mortars?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that. All I know was that UNPROFOR used the term "81" in respect of our mortars as well; although, we never had an 81-millimetre mortar. I think that the NATO standard was 81 and that the JNA standard was 82 and that that was the only difference. So both of these exist but with no significant difference between the two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you told us on Friday that your brigade never received an official protest, which you then characterised as being one from any of the United Nations forces. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your brigade ever receive any type of written protest from any source?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Protest? No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your brigade ever receive any type of oral protest from any source?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that would include either from superior units in the Sarajevo Romanija Corps or from the United Nations? Would that be -- would that be right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you told us also on Friday that your unit did not have uniforms at the beginning of the war. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it's also right that most able-bodied men in the former Yugoslavia served in either the military reserves or in the police reserves; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that those individuals who were serving in a reserve capacity in the JNA reserve would have had uniforms at home, so that if they were recalled they would have those uniforms available; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat what I stated on Friday: Partly, yes, they did. But generally, no. A large number of them didn't have such uniforms. These uniforms were sometimes worn privately, when people went to work. Some of these uniforms were returned to the units where these people had their assignments. So yes, some of them had them, but the majority didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you also told us on Friday that you were aware of paramilitary groups operating in your brigade's area of responsibility. Do you know where these groups were operating?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that I had known that. I knew that they existed de facto and were active in the area of responsibility of the brigade. But for a very brief period of time. I said that I remembered that we were the first unit of this corps that had eliminated the problem for good and probably the only one until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What steps did you take, if any, to alert the corps commander at the beginning when you realised you had this problem that this problem existed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I didn't alert the corps commander, in particular General Galic, at all, because by the time he arrived the problem had been solved for good. But before General Galic arrived, there was General Sipcic, whom I didn't alert either. I mean, I never saw him. It all went through the Vogosca Tactical Group and its commander. I insisted there with him and drew his attention to the problems. There were even some arrests that were carried out by them because our unit was not able to do it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know on the basis of your attendance at meetings involving the corps leadership what other areas paramilitary forces may have been operating in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were such forces in the corps's area of responsibility. Well, it was an interesting phenomenon. It all depended on what you considered to be a paramilitary unit. As far as I'm concerned, paramilitary units are all those units who are not subordinated to either the regular military unit in their area or the regular police unit deployed in their area. They had to be either under the Ministry of Defence, that is, the main staff or the corps, or the Ministry of the Interior. If that was not the case, then automatically this unit would be considered as a paramilitary unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall discussions at Lukavica barracks or elsewhere where General Galic was in attendance that the problem of paramilitary forces operating anywhere within the Sarajevo Romanija Corps's area of responsibility was discussed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It was a big problem which occurred on several occasions throughout a longer period of time. The issue was -- let me be specific. Let's take the example of the Kosevo Brigade. Throughout the war, for as long as it existed as a brigade and as a battalion, we never had a Praga weapon. A civilian may have had it; I don't know. There were such weapons at the beginning of the war, several multi-barrel weapons, and it was requested that these people, these individuals be placed under an appropriate command. It was a chain of events. If you have a parapolice unit, then of course you will end up having paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Witness, my final question for today: What steps did you take within your brigade to stop paramilitary activities in your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We first tried to place all these units under appropriate control in a normal manner. That is, we tried to involve their commanders in the defence, to ensure that they carry out the usual assignments, the usual tasks normally performed by any military or police in the world. But they refused it. After that, I attempted through the command of the tactical group -- that is, the operative group at the time to secure arrests, which indeed took place. Several individuals were arrested and then -- but this was just a make-shift prison. They were in custody only for several days for as long as it could be ensured by the commander of the tactical group. The problem therefore persisted, and in the end the Vogosca Tactical Group commander issued a written order on the basis of my request to remove them from the area of responsibility of the brigade, and they moved to another area of responsibility because he was simply unable to remove them from the tactical group for good, permanently. They were simply moved to another zone, but they were no longer in the area of the Kosevo Brigade when it was transformed into a battalion as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the time, and I think we've come to the end for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn until tomorrow morning. But I informed the parties already that next Friday there will be no change for other reasons. We're not able to meet the request.
